title: Walk modestly, lower your voice
hookLine: don't turn your cheek in scorn, walk modestly, lower your voice (31:18–19)

cards: Some people announce their importance before saying a word. They take up the middle of the corridor. They half-turn their face away when someone they consider beneath them starts talking.
They take the phone call at full volume in the train carriage. Luqman's advice to his son ends not with doctrine but with exactly this: how to hold your face, how to walk, and how loud to be.

teach.h: TURN NOT THY CHEEK IN SCORN.
teach.b: Luqman has told his son to pray, to enjoin what's right, to forbid what's wrong, and to be patient with what befalls him. Then he gets physical.
Pickthall: "Turn not thy cheek in scorn toward folk, nor walk with pertness in the land." The Arabic for turning the cheek is tusa''ir khaddak.
Classical lexicons say sa'ar was a condition in camels that made them twist their necks to one side. So picture a head permanently turned away from others, as if they're not worth facing.
Walking with pertness is marahan: strutting, walking in exultation. God doesn't love, the verse says, every arrogant boaster. Then the positive version.
Pickthall: "Be modest in thy bearing and subdue thy voice."
The first word is iqsid, from the same root as qasd, the middle, moderation: not crawling, not strutting, a steady pace aimed somewhere.

And lower your voice, ughdud, the same verb the Qur'an uses for lowering the gaze. Then a line that sticks: the harshest of all voices is the braying of the donkey. Loudness for its own sake isn't strength; it's noise.
This isn't a rule against ever raising your voice. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ called out to warn, and the call to prayer is meant to carry.
It's about posture toward people: a face that turns toward them, a walk that doesn't take over the street, and a voice sized to the room.

how: Muslims often teach Luqman's last pieces of advice, 31:17–19, as a short guide to manners: prayer, patience, humility, a moderate walk and a lowered voice.

o: walking slowly so others can pass you by
a quick pace, to show you have somewhere to be
a steady pace, neither strutting nor crawling

p: turning the cheek away in scorn

s: the verse forbids ever raising your voice

games.q: you're Luqman, ending your advice to your son. you've covered God, prayer and patience. what's left?
o: how to hold your face, walk, and speak.
games.why: 31:18–19: don't turn your cheek in scorn, don't strut, be modest in bearing and lower your voice.

practice: Notice your face right now, whether it's turned toward anything or away, and let it soften.

Then bring to mind the place where you're usually loudest, the kitchen, a meeting, the car, a group chat in capital letters, and replay that moment with your voice at half and your face toward the other person.
If you pray, you can ask for a gentle voice.

wordCard.voice: Walk modestly. Luqman's advice on how to carry yourself: don't turn your cheek in scorn, don't strut, keep a steady pace, and lower your voice. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: 'be moderate in your walk', from the root of qasd, the middle way.
